# Contract-call characterisation fixtures

These fixtures pin what the SDK does today when it talks to a contract, so a
change to the call path can be shown to leave requests and wire bytes alone and
to change results only where a test row says so. They record behaviour; they are
not a statement of what the behaviour should be.

## What is recorded

- `requests-pos.json`, `requests-staking.json`, `requests-plasma.json`: for each
  public method that reaches a contract, the requests it hands to the adapter,
  in order. Each request holds the side (`parent` or `child`), the kind (`read`,
  `write`, `prepareWrite` or `estimateGas`), the ABI's exported name, the
  address, the function, the block tag for a read, every write field (`from`,
  `value`, `gasLimit`, fee caps, `nonce`, `chainId`), and each argument as
  `{ type, value }`. The type matters: an adapter sees a `bigint`, a hex
  `string` or a `number` differently, and an argument that changes from one to
  another is a change a consumer's own adapter can observe. A `bigint` is tagged
  `{ "$bigint": "123" }`, as in `tests/unit/cassette-adapter.ts`.
- `read-wire.json`: for each contract read the SDK makes, the `eth_call`
  requests (`to`, `data`, block tag) that reach the node and the value the
  public method returns. The same row is checked against viem, ethers v5 and
  ethers v6, so the three libraries must send the same bytes and the method must
  return the same value on each.

## How the files are generated, and why

The request and wire files are generated by the tests that read them, once, from
the code as it is, and then committed. A normal run only compares. To
regenerate:

```sh
WRITE_CONTRACT_CALL_FIXTURES=1 pnpm --filter @polygonlabs/maticjs exec vitest run \
  tests/unit/contract-requests-pos.test.ts \
  tests/unit/contract-requests-staking.test.ts \
  tests/unit/contract-requests-plasma.test.ts \
  tests/unit/contract-read-wire.test.ts
```

Generating from the code is the point: the fixtures are meant to say what the
code does, not what someone expects it to do, so they are never written by
hand. For the same reason, regenerate only on a base these suites are meant to
describe, and read the diff before committing it. A diff in a fixture is the
complete list of what changed in the requests or the wire bytes.

## Conventions that keep the files reviewable

- A string longer than 200 characters is an exit payload (kilobytes of proof).
  It is recorded as `{ "$keccak256": "<hash of the bytes>", "length": <n> }`, so
  any changed byte still shows.
- The exit paths binary-search the checkpoint headers, so a recorded burn
  produces dozens of `headerBlocks` reads whose arguments come from the
  recording. For those scenarios only the first read of each function, block tag
  and argument-type signature is kept; the writes are what they pin.
- Exit scenarios replay RPC responses recorded under `tests/fixtures/exits`.
  They need no network.

## Coverage

Each request suite lists the contract methods the SDK calls and fails when a
method has no row in its fixture, or has a write row without its `prepareWrite`
sibling. A new call site therefore needs a scenario. The scenario names in the
fixtures and in the tests must match, so a renamed or deleted scenario fails
instead of silently shrinking the comparison.

## Result shapes

`contract-result-shapes-*.test.ts` hold the third kind of pin. They have no
fixture file: each table lists, in the test, what a public read does with every
shape a contract call can return (well formed or not). A row whose outcome today
is a native error, a wrong answer, or an SDK error that names the malformed
value differently from how a validating read will carries the comment
`// changes when the read is decoded`. Only those rows may be edited when reads
start validating their results; every other row must stay as it is.
